I can see that there is a sharp rise in the % of weekly doctor and hospital visits for upper respiratory diseases (URD) in 2022-2023 and this could be due to the resurgence of URD not only by COVID but also RSV and flu. This could make sense since people used to wear masks before to protect themselves from COVID but that is not the case anymore as mask mandates were repealed. 
the next sharp rise was during 2019-2020 and we see the sharp rise but there is more variability and oscillation of the graph due to mask mandates, isolations, and then relaxation of the mandates and quarantine measures. 
The general trend indicates that the % of weekly doctors and hospitalization increases every Dec-January. That could be exacerbated due to the winter and cold temperatures and how our immunity has to adapt to the new temperatures and the rise of respiratory illnesses. Interestingly,  the lowest % is in 2020-2021 due to isolation/quarantine and mask mandates as well as the fact that people were vaccinated at the time. 
This affects my community as we are getting ready to go to work and many people are not wearing masks at work or even at the gym where there is so much closeness.

1) What do you notice?

Additionally, according to data from 2022–2023, there was a noticeable increase from October to November that appeared to be continuing.

1. Until 2022-2023, the winter season was the busiest time for doctors and hospital visits regarding respiratory illnesses. Could the results of people being positive for COVID be the cause of the decrease in 2021-2022 and then cause an increase in 2022-2023?
3. This relates to my community and me because my father was hospitalized for COVID which caused him to have permanent damage to his lungs and respiratory issues that are being treated. For my community, it affected many people leaving them with treatable or untreatable damage to their respiratory systems. This virus caused a worldwide shut down from how contagious it was. It caused schools to close down and continue instruction virtually for about 2 years, people to work from home, or to be laid off from work, and small businesses to close down. How do we know that same won't happen again?

1. I notice that in 2020-2021, the trend for hospital and doctor visits was the lowest compared to 2019-2020 and 2021-2022, and even 2022-2023. I also notice that in 2021-2022, there was a peak in visits in January and then slopes down after. Also, from what data was recorded in 2022-2023, there is a sharp increase from October to November and seems to be continuing to increase. 

2. I wonder why in the years 2021-2022 it seems to have the greatest amount of visits if within these years COVID cases were going down during this time? I also wonder why there was a sudden spike in visits during 2022-2023 when the COVID era is basically over. Also, during this time, was there any created paranoia about COVID cases afterward?

3. This relates to my community because COVID has hit the city of Perth Amboy hard, and has led to a lot of paranoia over the years. This directly correlates to the graph because before COVID started and it was ever really heard of, people were starting to get paranoid and frequently checked themselves to make sure they were healthy. When COVID hit our city, many people were too scared to go out in order to seek help or even get groceries from the stores. Afterward, people started to get paranoid once again to make sure no one reignited the pandemic and sought to not get themselves sick due to the tragedies it caused.

1. The title I would give this graph is, "Can Paranoia Influence Doctor's Visits?"

I wonder if the amount of respiratory diseases are caught mostly by only a small amount of the population which has been careless over their personal health since the "end" of the pandemic, or if the increase of respiratory diseases are a trend for the whole population?

This might relate to my community since our community is especially densely populated, so any sickness could easily quickly spread throughout a school, office, or health facility. This could also be a sign of changing attitudes to "regular" respiratory diseases, such as the flu. Heightened fear of Covid-19 might have reduced fear for other diseases. 

The Problem of Complacence in a Post-Pandemic World

If the data for 2022-23 was represented differently where different categories separating people infected with influenza, COVID-19, etc was shown, would it have shown that a specific virus was pulling the data to go higher? 3. My community and I can relate to this data of weekly doctor and hospital visits for respiratory illness because the most recent virus, COVID-19, affected many people, including my family. I've had family hospitalized because of respiratory problems, which was a very emotional time. So, seeing the rise of doctor and hospital visits for respiratory illnesses makes me worry if something is going on again.

comments.raw_comment:
1) Until 2022-23, the winter months were often the busiest for doctor and hospital visits for respiratory diseases. Pre-pandemic visits were roughly 5.5% from late December to January. The year 2022-23 is notable, with occurrences increasing much earlier, from October to December - from around 2.5% to over 7.5%, the highest point on the curve. I notice there is a triple peak in the 2019-2020 season around 7%. 

2) Did prior years' diseases such as influenza, covid 19, and so on have long-term consequences on the respiratory system, influencing the 2022-2023 report? I'm curious why the lowest percentage of weekly doctor and hospital visits occurred in 2020-21, when it was intended to be the peak of Covid-19. Why is there a triple peak for the 2019-2020 season? I wonder if immunities gained from the pandemic had an impact on doctor visits post-pandemic.

3) During the winter season, disease seems to afflict the planet, and it is easy to witness sickness in high school. Masks are uncommon at this stage after the epidemic, and it's strange to feel as though disease surrounds me and I'm at the eye of the storm. Relatives of mine have had tremendous difficulty overcoming illnesses brought on by weather and transmuted by pathogens from coworkers. As someone who has had to constantly observe and be a patient at the doctor's and hospital, it's intriguing to find me amid a sea of individuals who are similar to me.

4) The Doctor's In! A History of Respiratory Illness Fluctuations

1) I notice that the graph is demonstrating the rates of how many people visited hospitals before, during, and after (sort of) the pandemic. The dotted line represents the pre pandemic weekly average of doctor/hospital visits for respiratory illness. In 2019-2020, there was a substantial increase in visits, and during the peak of the pandemic, there was a substantial growth between January and April. In the years of 2020-2021 and 2021-22, there happens to appear a great decrease in the visits compared to before the pandemic started.  This is probably due to lockdown and vast self-testing. Folks could have been afraid to visit hospitals in fear that they would also catch any viruses while there. However, during 2022-2023, there is a great increase in the visits.
2) What I wonder is what initially increased visits in 2021-22, but then began to decline once it reached March-April. And will this year follow in the footsteps of the past 3 years? Where the visit rates increase by a lot but decrease as spring rolls around.  
3) This relates to me and my community because COVID and other respiratory illnesses have affected myself, friends, and family. As well as the rest of the world. And because of this, just like everyone else, we were put in lockdown. And the only times we were really allowed out was whenever we had to rush to the hospital (for a REAL emergency) or for grocery shopping. 
4) Are the last three years' worth of lung failure entirely Covid's fault?

What do you notice?: 
I noticed that out of all the years, on November 26th, doctor visits for respiratory illness were the highest for the year 2022. And it’s also the highest overall peak compared to the other lines on any other day. I also noticed that around April of 2020, the percentage of visits went down sharply, which is also around the time when the quarantine began. It’s most likely that because people began to take care of themselves more by wearing masks or staying inside, there was less of a need for any visits. Now in recent times since people have started being less cautious and wearing masks less, the number of visits have begun to increase again.

What do you wonder?:
I wonder why things like mask regulations were removed when in the graph, it shows that there were less visits during the pandemic than after it, meaning it was beneficial to a degree. I also wonder if most of the recent visits are mainly due to COVID or if it’s an equal mix of it with the influenza and other respiratory illnesses.

How does this relate to you and your community?:
This relates to my community and I because there are a lot of people around me that are currently getting sick. Especially in a school environment with a large number of students and teachers walking around, it’s very easy to spread these illnesses to others if the proper precautions aren’t taken.

What do I notice? 
- Around the time of the COVID-19 pandemic, (especially 2019-2020) doctor/ hospital visits related to respiratory illness relatively heightened compared to the pre-pandemic average. 
- In 2022 and 2023, the visits were at an all time high regarding percentage (despite not being in the worst part of COVID in the US). 
- Respiratory visit percentages tend to peak around colder months (October through April), and begin to go down during the summer with warmer weather. 
What do I wonder? 
- What specific respiratory visits are included in these percentages? 
- What led to the visits being able to so drastically go down in 2022-21, despite COVID still being a concern? 
What do I think is going on in this graph? 
I think this graph is displaying the percentages of respiratory related visits to the hospital between the years of 2019 and 2023 (only November 2022, but the graph includes 2023). The graph begins around the fall and ends near the summer. 
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because, in middle school when COVID-19 became very serious, the first people who had to quarantine were those with respiratory conditions such as asthma.

I noticed that the 2019-20 weekly visit was the highest in late December through the end of April. Than the average had decreased exponentially with an all time low throughout 2020-21. The early winter was also shown to be the time that the average pre-pandemic respiratory illnesses spiked. The 2022-23 respiratory illnesses has been the highest than it has ever been earlier than average. This could be because people's respiratory systems had been weakened from the pandemic, resulting in being more susceptible to respiratory illnesses.

In my own community I have seen a rise in colds earlier than normal, for the winter season.

Today’s graph displays past and present trends of respiratory illness – flu, Covid and R.S.V., during the course of cold seasons.   This year’s trend looks like a doozy, outpacing recent past years.

comments.raw_comment:
1. Prior to 2022-23, the winter months were frequently the busiest for doctor and hospital visits for respiratory disorders. For example, prepandemic visits were approximately 5.5% from late December to January; for the same period in 2019-20, visits were approximately 6.5% just as coronavirus was beginning; 2020-21 visits were approximately 1.5%, likely due to quarantine and then masking, with little virus circulating; and 2021-22 visits were just under 5%. in accordance with pre pandemic levels. 2022-23 is remarkable, with incidences increasing substantially earlier, from October to December - from roughly 2.5% to over 7.5%, the highest point of any year on the graph. 
2. I'm curious if the repeal of the mask mandate is one of the reasons contributing to the dramatic spike in medical visits. Is Covid-19 the most common respiratory virus reported due to the numerous strains detected every day? 
3. This is relevant to me and my community since COVID has taken a toll not just on the entire planet but also on my family. Despite being exceedingly cautious and following the CDC's instructions, several of my family members have become ill as a result of the virus. Social distance and masking were just a minor factor in keeping the virus at bay, since many individuals refused to put on their masks and learn the hard way that the illness is exceedingly dangerous. 
4. Trouble Breathing: A Spike in Doctor Visits Indicates an Increase in Respiratory Viruses...Are You the Next Patient?

comments.raw_comment:
1.  Prior to 2022-23, the peak for doctor and hospital visits for respiratory illnesses generally occurred in winter months.  For example, during late Dec through Jan., prepandemic visits were approximately 5.5%; for the same period 2019-20 visits were approximately 6.5% (right as coronavirus was starting); 2020-21 visits were approx 1.5% (this was likely so low because of quarantine and then masking, not much virus circulating); and 2021-22 visits were just under 5% (in line with prepandemic levels).  2022-23 seems unusual with cases trending steeply upward early, from Oct-Dec -- from approx 2.5% to approx 7.5%, highest point of any year on graph.
2.  I wonder why cases in 2022-23 rose so high -- higher than ever before -- so quickly and so much earlier than in prior years.  I also wonder what steps can be taken to help stop the increase (more vaccines?  A return to masking?).
3.  My family and I have all gotten our flu and covid shots soI feel pretty confident that if we do get sick we will be ok.  But I worry that if there are that many sick people these illnesses will spread more easily and people like my grandmother -- who has lung cancer and other underlying health conditions -- will be at greater risk of getting seriously sick.  I also wonder whether our school district will begin making us wear masks again if rates of respiratory illness are very high in our community.

1) What do you notice?
The first thing I noticed is the recent (2022-23) spike in percent of weekly doctor/hospital visits for respiratory illnesses in the U.S- the highest spike/only one to pass around 7%. Typically, the highest percents tend to be between January and April, reaching lower numbers after April. I also noticed that between 2020 and 2021, the graph was the most consistent with only minor increases or decreases, while the others tended to have drastically high spikes in the percentages. Something that sticks out to me about the dates is that they span across the years of Covid-19. 
2) What do you wonder?
Lifting the mask mandate inevitably caused hospital visit numbers to rise, but I wonder if there were any other factors that caused such a large spike in recent years?
3) How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because more hospital/doctor visits mean more people feeling ill/testing positive for various illnesses, so it is our job to keep protecting ourselves and those around us.
4) What’s going on in this graph?
This graph shows the percent of weekly doctor/hospital visits for respiratory illnesses in the U.S. My headline would be: New Year Means New Highs in Hospital Visits.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed in the graph that there is a spike in the amount of doctor visits for respiratory illnesses in October 2022 - Now January 2023. This spike is higher than it was during March 2019- July 2022. It shows that 7% of weekly doctor visits are for respiratory illnesses. I wonder what caused this spike. Could it be because of a surge of RSV, COVID, and influenza happening at the same time? It could be caused by the mask mandate being lifted, because during Jan 2020-21 the mask mandate was still in order in most states in the U.S. and we can see that the percentage of doctors visits were less than 2%. People are more inclined to catch a cold during the winter season because of the weather. Many people are also inclined to travel during the holidays and go to holiday parties, where there is a high risk of the spreading of these illnesses. A lot of activists also happen indoor in the winter, and when these gatherings are in a tight place with no air flow, the spread of these viruses tend to spread quickly. I have noticed in my community a lot of people in my community getting sick from RSV and COVID during the holiday season. In stores I see many people start to wear masks again, so they can protect themselves and their families from these illnesses going around. The spike in these illnesses were bound to happen especially with the holiday season.“Not Again….Spike in Respiratory Illnesses”

comments.raw_comment:
What I notice is that 2020-21 was pretty calm, there weren't big fluctuations which means there were not as many people visiting the hospital/doctors because of respiratory illness. At the start of the pandemic it impacted a lot of people and that led to more people visiting the doctor. I noticed it almost reaches the pandemic average in 2021-22, but then there’s a huge drop. In 2022-23 I can see the rise and how many people have actually started to visit the hospital, it’s almost matching the beginning of the pandemic in 2019 when it was bad. 
What I wonder is why are there so many people in 2022-23 going to the hospital for respiratory illnesses, is it a new strain of COVID or a new disease. In 2019-20 there’s a huge increase. My question is were people just going to hospital because they were scared and worried that any respiratory illness was COVID or were there actual cases? Maybe the amount of cases dropped through the years because people self tested or didn’t want the stigma of having COVID. 
This relates to me and my community because they were impacted by respiratory illnesses which include COVID and the other strains of it. 1) What do you noticed?

As the years have gone on, the peak of illness has been lasting longer, with an exception for 2020-21. 2020-21 appears to be the lowest year because we had a lockdown, so many people were not getting sick, or weren't going to the doctor. We wonder if there will be a truly effective treatment for COVID. We also wonder what will happen in the future if illness continues to spread like this. Will there be future mask requirement and lockdowns? 

3) How does this relate to you and your community?

People are getting sick more frequently; most of us have been affected by at least one of these illnesses.
